questions.q: What's the main problem with compiling a Go binary using a single-stage Dockerfile based on `golang:1.23`?
options: The final shipped image includes the entire Go toolchain and build environment underneath the binary, even though none of it is needed at runtime
golang:1.23 cannot run a compiled binary, only interpret Go source directly
Single-stage builds are not supported by current versions of Docker
go build cannot be run inside any Dockerfile, regardless of stages
questions.explain: Nothing in a single-stage build removes the base image's layers, so the full compiler, standard library source, and build caches all ship inside the final image alongside the actual binary.

questions.q: In `FROM golang:1.23 AS build`, what does `AS build` do?
options: It tells Docker to delete this stage automatically once the Dockerfile finishes building
It names this stage `build` so a later stage can reference it, e.g. with `COPY --from=build`
It forces this stage to run after every other stage in the file
It marks this stage as the one that will be tagged by `docker build -t`
questions.explain: AS <name> is just a label on a stage. It lets a later COPY --from=<name> instruction reach back into that stage's filesystem; it has no effect on execution order or which stage gets tagged.

questions.q: In a multi-stage Dockerfile, what determines what `docker build -t myapp .` actually tags as the final image?
options: The stage containing the most RUN instructions
Whichever stage is named `build`, regardless of position
The final `FROM` instruction in the file, unless `--target` points at an earlier stage instead
All stages are merged together into one final image automatically
questions.explain: docker build runs every stage, but the final FROM in the file is what gets tagged by default. --target lets you build and tag an earlier stage instead, which is useful for inspecting an intermediate build stage directly.

questions.q: In the multi-stage Node.js example, why does the `runtime` stage run its own `npm ci --omit=dev` instead of copying `node_modules` forward from the `build` stage?
options: npm ci cannot run more than once across the lifetime of a Dockerfile
Copying node_modules between stages is required by npm and cannot be skipped
COPY --from cannot copy directories, only single files
Resolving its own production-only dependency tree avoids mixing dev and production installs between stages, a common source of subtly broken runtime images
questions.explain: The build stage needs devDependencies (bundlers, compilers) to produce dist/. The runtime stage only needs production dependencies, so it resolves its own clean install rather than inheriting a mixed dependency tree from build.

questions.q: What does switching the final stage's base image to a `distroless` image buy you, once the application's build artifact no longer depends on the build stage's base image?
options: Faster `docker build` times across every stage in the Dockerfile
Automatic multi-architecture support with no other configuration
A smaller attack surface: no shell and no package manager for an attacker with code execution inside the container to use
Guaranteed compatibility with every native Node or Go module without exception
questions.explain: Once build and runtime environments are decoupled, the runtime base can be chosen purely for running the artifact safely and minimally — distroless images strip out the shell and package manager that would otherwise give an attacker more to work with.
